title: Latvia Installs New PM After Drone Incidents Topple Coalition
summary: Latvia has a new prime minister after a dispute over wayward drones brought down the previous government. On Thursday, lawmakers confirmed 47-year-old centrist Andris Kulbergs by a vote of 66 to 34, tasking him with leading the Baltic nation of 1.8 million until elections on October 3. The crisis began when multiple drones, suspected to be Ukrainian attack drones knocked off course by Russian jamming, crossed into Latvian territory. They caused minimal damage but ignited public alarm in the former Soviet republic, now a NATO and EU member. Former Prime Minister Evika Silina resigned in mid-May after her coalition partner withdrew support, blaming Defence Minister Andris Spruds for not deploying anti-drone defenses quickly enough. Silina said Spruds had lost her trust and that of the public. Kulbergs, who had backing from President Edgars Rinkevics, now leads a four-party coalition with a healthy majority. In his speech, he stressed that the government’s duty is to ensure Latvia’s security “in the broadest sense”—external, economic, energy, and people’s sense of safety. The coalition parties have emphasized reinforcing the military and borders. Political scientist Nils Muiznieks noted a “broad consensus on foreign policy priorities,” meaning the new government will likely maintain strong solidarity with Ukraine and a pro-Western stance. The drone incidents are not isolated; several Russian and Ukrainian drones have crashed in Latvia and neighboring Lithuania and Estonia since Russia’s 2022 invasion. For Latvia, a country that regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, the war next door is a constant reminder of its own history. The new government faces the challenge of navigating security threats while preparing for elections in just over four months.
why_it_matters: This story reveals how even small incidents like stray drones can topple a government in a country on NATO's front line, highlighting the fragility of security and the importance of alliances when war is literally next door—a reminder that global events can shake local politics overnight.

background_read: Latvia, along with its Baltic neighbors Lithuania and Estonia, was part of the Soviet Union until 1991, when it regained independence. All three countries joined NATO and the European Union in 2004, placing them directly on the frontline between the Western alliance and Russia.

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the Baltic states have been on high alert. Several Russian and Ukrainian drones have crashed on their territories, a reminder that the war is not far away. These stray drones are often the result of jamming, electronic countermeasures that disrupt a drone’s control signals, causing it to veer off course.

Andris Kulbergs, a centrist who previously held other government roles, now leads a four-party coalition with a solid majority. President Edgars Rinkevics (Latvia’s head of state, with a mostly ceremonial role) backed his appointment. The fall of former Prime Minister Evika Silina’s government highlights how even a few wayward unmanned aircraft can trigger a political crisis in a small, security-focused country.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Latvia installs new Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs after a drone-related dispute toppled the previous government.
└─ VOTE: Confirmed 66 to 34, leading a four-party coalition until October elections.

├─ ORIGIN: Russian electronic interference may have redirected the drones.
└─ EFFECT: Minimal physical damage but maximum public alarm in the former Soviet republic.

├─ REASON: Defence Minister Andris Spruds failed to deploy anti-drone defenses quickly enough.
└─ TRUST LOST: Silina said the minister lost her trust and the public’s confidence.
NEW GOVERNMENT’S FOCUS: Kulbergs stressed security in the broadest sense—external, economic, energy, and psychological.
└─ COALITION CONSENSUS: Pro-Western foreign policy and solidarity with Ukraine.
EXPERT VIEW: Political scientist Nils Muiznieks notes a broad foreign policy consensus.
└─ IMPLICATION: Latvia will continue a strong pro-Ukraine and pro-NATO stance.
HISTORICAL CONTEXT: Drone incursions are not new; since 2022 both Russian and Ukrainian drones have crashed in the Baltic region. Latvia’s Soviet past makes the war feel immediate.
OPEN QUESTION: Can the new government quickly strengthen defenses and win voter confidence before elections in four months?

perspectives.description: The swift formation of a four-party coalition with a healthy majority ensures political stability and continuity of Latvia’s strong support for Ukraine and NATO. Having a clear mandate may allow the government to speed up military and border reinforcement, reassuring allies and citizens.

The drone incident revealed serious gaps in national defense preparedness; the previous government’s slow anti-drone response and the resulting political chaos raise doubts. Critics worry that internal squabbling distracts from the immediate threat environment and that the new cabinet may face the same bureaucratic hurdles.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical (systemic pressure on small states)
perspectives.description: The fall of a government over a defense dispute illustrates how external security crises can rapidly reshape domestic politics in small NATO states bordering Russia. It is part of a broader pattern in the Baltic region, where hybrid threats—jamming, drone incursions, and disinformation—are used to test and destabilize societies.

With elections only four months away, the new government must quickly demonstrate it can handle hybrid threats and bolster public confidence, or risk being replaced again by voters. The outcome will influence whether Latvia maintains its hawkish foreign policy or faces internal pressure to prioritize domestic concerns.
